# Start writing {#start-writing .divider background-color="#23373B"}

::: {.roadmap}
[Start writing](#start-writing){.current} [The introduction](#the-introduction) [Structure](#structure) [Storytelling](#storytelling) [Rules](#rules)
:::


# Getting started

When should you start writing?

::: {.steps}
1. You have an idea and given it some real thought
2. Your "scaffolding" is built
3. Your data are organized and nearly ready
:::

. . .

::: {.big}
Write your introduction.
:::

::: {.notes}
Ask who has already written an introduction for their third-year paper, and who has written anything at all yet.
:::


# First draft intro

:::: {.cards .two}
::: {.card}
**❌ This introduction is NOT**

- Final
- Particularly well-informed
- Accurate
:::
::: {.card}
**✅ This introduction IS**

- What you **want** to do
- What you **think** is the contribution
- How you'd **like** to proceed
:::
::::

. . .

What would your paper look like if everything works out perfectly? This is the "aspirational introduction" as per Shapiro's [four steps to writing an applied paper](https://shapiro.scholars.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum7731/files/2026-02/foursteps.pdf)


# What it looks like

Four sentences. Shapiro's advice is that you can make up the results, within reason.

::: {.steps}
1. **The issue.** [The issue] matters because [who it affects, and how].
2. **The question.** This paper asks whether [specific question].
3. **The approach.** We use [data] and [design] to [what you will do].
4. **The answer.** We find [the result you hope for], which means [why anyone should care].
:::


# Using the first draft intro

This should become your guide to the paper

- What analyses are you going to run?
- What summary statistics/figures tell a good story?
- What other work has already been done?
- What are the weakest parts of your project/analysis?


# What to write next

The introduction tells you what the paper needs. One order that works:

::::: {.flow}
:::: {.step}
📊

**Data and setting**

You already know these
::::
:::: {.arrow}
→
::::
:::: {.step}
🧮

**Empirical approach**

What the introduction said you would do
::::
:::: {.arrow}
→
::::
:::: {.step}
📈

**Results**

As the estimates come in
::::
:::: {.arrow}
→
::::
:::: {.step}
🏁

**Conclusion, then abstract**

Last, once you know what you found
::::
:::::


# Make time

- You have to make time to do it!
- Some strategies to consider:
  - Block at least one hour in the mornings to write
  - Set specific goals (write the data section, add robustness check, etc.)
  - Organize writing sessions or retreats

. . .

Staring at the screen for 15 minutes without writing? Take a break and come back to it.


# When nothing is coming

- Write a rough version now and fix it tomorrow
- Start with a figure: write the caption, then the paragraph that explains it
- Explain the result to a classmate, then write down what you said
- Write one paragraph, then the next


# Main point

- No one writes perfectly in the first draft
- Most of what you write will change
- Think of writing very early drafts as a more informed and organized brainstorming session


# The introduction {#the-introduction .divider background-color="#23373B"}

::: {.roadmap}
[Start writing](#start-writing) [The introduction](#the-introduction){.current} [Structure](#structure) [Storytelling](#storytelling) [Rules](#rules)
:::


# Introduction {.center}

::: {.big}
The introduction is the most important thing you'll write for any paper.
:::

. . .

Make it awesome!


# Introduction [formula](https://www.albany.edu/spatial/training/5-The%20Introduction%20Formula.pdf)

::: {.steps .incremental}
1. **The Hook.** Why should anyone care about this at all? What big issue are you dealing with?
2. **Question.** What are you actually going to do? What is your actual research question? Doesn't need context.
3. **Context.** What are the key things that other people have done? What literature should a reader know in order to understand your contribution?
4. **Contribution.** What are you doing differently? Should be in context of the existing literature.
5. **Expand.** I've added this. Modern applied papers (for better or worse) need to talk about some key additional findings in the intro (mechanisms, robustness, and policy implications, etc.).
:::

# Paper structure

We've all seen the "standard" applied econ paper structure:

::::: {.columns}
:::: {.column width="50%"}
::: {.steps}
1. Introduction
2. Theoretical motivation or institutional details
3. Data
4. Estimation
5. Results
6. Conclusion
:::
::::
:::: {.column width="50%" .fragment}
I **do not** like this formula...

- Fine as outline
- Too rigid and boring
- Need better **story**
::::
:::::


# Paper structure

- Take a look at (almost) any top applied paper in the last several years
- Most will start similarly (intro, theory/policy details, maybe data)
- Deviate based on relevant analyses and estimation strategies


# Writing steps

Following Jesse Shapiro's [four steps to an applied paper](https://shapiro.scholars.harvard.edu/sites/g/files/omnuum7731/files/2026-02/foursteps.pdf)...

::::: {.flow}
:::: {.step}
1️⃣

**Aspirational introduction**

We've already done this
::::
:::: {.arrow}
→
::::
:::: {.step}
2️⃣

**Research**

Not part of this workshop
::::
:::: {.arrow .fragment}
→
::::
:::: {.step .fragment}
3️⃣

**Be a robot**

Linear, clear, plain, and formal. Back to (2) as you find gaps
::::
:::: {.arrow .fragment}
→
::::
:::: {.step .fragment}
4️⃣

**Contractual introduction**

Rewrite the intro as a contract for what the paper will and won't do. Back to (2) and (3) as needed
::::
:::::

# Storytelling

- Like it or not, you have to **sell** your work
- Can be hard and can feel antithetical to the "objective" scientific process
- But we're humans and we need to be entertained!

![](https://media.giphy.com/media/hrnYspWWhsIyA/source.gif){fig-align="center"}


# Storytelling

So how do we write something compelling? Try [paper writing gone hollywood](https://www.science.org/doi/10.1126/science.355.6320.102)...

- A general outline isn't enough
- Need to "storyboard" each section or subsection
- Rely heavily on outlines rather than getting bogged down in verbiage

::: {.roadmap}
[Start writing](#start-writing) [The introduction](#the-introduction) [Structure](#structure) [Storytelling](#storytelling) [Rules](#rules){.current}
:::


# Some rules

Finally, let's close things out with some simple [rules](https://www.economics.harvard.edu/resource/tenruleswritingpdf), courtesy of Claudia Goldin and Lawrence Katz.


# Some rules

I'll add a few to these...

::: {.steps}
1. Be careful with self-plagiarism (also with normal plagiarism)
2. Write the abstract. **Do not** copy and paste from the intro, or vice versa.
3. Use "I" if you're the only author. Use "we" otherwise.
4. Define the acronym the first time only, then just use it.
:::


. . .

Seriously, don't copy and paste your own words from another paper. Be more creative than that. And definitely don't copy someone else's words.

Below are a few links to papers that are generally thought to be extremely well-written:
